title: Rule of three, five, then zero
summary: A double close, copies deleted, moves added, then unique_ptr takes all five away.

turns.user: put LogFile in a vector and it double closes at shutdown. there IS a destructor

assistant.body: The implicit copy constructor copies fp_ as it stands, so two objects close the same handle. Writing a destructor means you own the copy operations too. Start by banning the copy.

LogFile(const LogFile&) = delete;
LogFile& operator=(const LogFile&) = delete;

turns.user: builds, but now push_back does not compile. someone said rule of three at me, is that this?

assistant.body: My fault, deleting the copies also suppresses the implicit move. Destructor plus the two copies is the rule of three, and the two moves on top make it five. push_back works once the moves exist.

turns.user: writing five of these by hand is a drag. can we get to rule of zero

assistant.body: A unique_ptr with a custom deleter throws all five away. sed swaps the member and the initializer and drops the destructor line. The & on the right side of a substitution means the whole match, so it gets escaped.
sed -i '' 's/std::FILE\* fp_;/std::unique_ptr<std::FILE, int (*)(std::FILE*)> fp_;/; s/"a"))/"a"), \&std::fclose)/; /~LogFile/d' src/log/log_file.h
Only write is left. The raw handle becomes get(), plus the include.

#include <memory>

void write(const std::string& line) { std::fputs(line.c_str(), fp_.get()); }
